Listen to this article Share …Commission plans dedicated AI division as stakeholders warn of deepfakes, fake results, digital voter manipulation The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) will establish a dedicated Artificial Intelligence Division to protect the 2027 general elections from deepfakes, disinformation and cyber threats, as Yiaga Africa and other stakeholders warn that AI manipulation could undermine voter confidence. The plan was unveiled Wednesday at the 2026 AI and Democracy Forum at the Transcorp Hilton, Abuja, organised by Yiaga Africa in partnership with INEC. The two-day forum, themed “Safeguarding the 2027 General Elections in the Age of Artificial Intelligence,” brought together electoral authorities, technology companies and civil society to develop practical safeguards ahead of the polls. Joash Amupitan, INEC Chairman used the forum to appeal to Nigerians to stop judging his leadership based on the experience of the 2023 general elections. He said his administration is focused on rebuilding trust through institutional reforms, transparent procedures and stronger safeguards, and should be assessed on the measures now being put in place for 2027. INEC said the new division, domiciled in its Information and Communications Technology Department, will give the commission institutional capacity to assess emerging technologies, manage associated risks and explore responsible applications, including data-driven risk assessment and election logistics. The commission is also working with technology and development partners on an AI governance framework. INEC’s position is that technology must support electoral administration without displacing human judgement or the will of voters. Read also: 2027: Kwankwasiyya raises alarm over NDC candidates’ omission in Kano Itodo warns of impersonation, fake results Executive Director of Yiaga Africa, Samson Itodo, said AI threats could no longer be treated as distant possibilities. “If AI is used to impersonate INEC officials or release fake election results, it could cause serious unrest,” Itodo warned. He said artificial intelligence has made it easier to manufacture convincing audio, video and images that can mislead voters and distort political debate, from false announcements of election results to manipulated recordings attributed to public officials. Microsoft, TikTok and the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) are among the partners supporting the gathering, underscoring the need for cooperation between election managers and digital platforms. ECONEC warns against algorithmic control The regional dimension was highlighted by Abdoulaye Sylla, chairperson of Senegal’s electoral commission and the ECOWAS Network of Electoral Commissions (ECONEC). “The challenge before us is therefore not whether artificial intelligence will influence our democracies, but how we can ensure that its use strengthens, rather than undermines, the credibility of our electoral processes,” Sylla said. “Technology must serve democracy, and not become a substitute for democratic accountability, independent institutions, or human judgement,” he added, stressing that electoral integrity must remain anchored in transparency, accountability, fairness and inclusion. Public trust will be the big test Beyond institutional reforms, stakeholders agreed that voter confidence will be decisive. INEC will need to explain how AI-assisted systems operate, what decisions they can influence, and what procedures exist to identify errors, prevent abuse and investigate interference. The speed and credibility of official communication will be critical when fabricated results or recordings circulate. The forum, which ends October 15, is expected to produce coordinated responses for electoral authorities, platforms and the media before the 2027 cycle gathers momentum.
